subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage: In a village hall outside Jhansi, Sachin ran a Saturday tuition centre for forty children. Every month he sat down with Preeti, a volunteer teacher, and a notebook. They counted attendance from the register, marked the short maths test, and asked each child for one line on what they liked and disliked. In March the reading circle had eleven children on average and scores had barely moved. The children's notes said, 'Story time is the best.' Maths practice had steady attendance and rising scores. The two decided: drop the drawing class, which had few children and no change in anything; change reading to use stories; keep maths as it was. Sachin pinned the numbers on the hall wall. 'We'll look again in April,' he said.

qa.q: How many children did the reading circle have on average in March?
qa.a: The reading circle had eleven children on average.

qa.q: What does Sachin want from looking at the numbers again in April?
qa.a: Sachin wants decisions to rest on evidence and to keep adjusting, which shows a steady commitment to the centre.

qa.q: What other kind of evidence could Sachin add to the monthly numbers?
qa.a: Sachin could ask parents at pick-up time what they notice at home, since families may see changes that scores and registers miss.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the decision to drop the drawing class?
qa.a: Preeti probably sees it as fair because the numbers back it, though may feel sorry for the few children who enjoyed it.

grounding: Shows an organiser recording attendance, test scores and student feedback each month and using them to decide whether to continue, adjust or stop each activity.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
On the first Monday of every month, Priscila spread three sheets across the kitchen table of the community flat in Porto. Attendance from the sign-in book. The short maths quiz the children took each Friday. And the feedback cards, where they drew a face and wrote one sentence.
Ulla, the volunteer who ran the chess hour, peered over her shoulder. "So? Are we keeping chess?"
Priscila tapped the numbers. "Chess has had three children for two months. The cards say it's 'fine.' Homework help has fourteen, and quiz scores went up from the last month."
"That's harsh on chess."
"Not stopping it yet. Let's try it on Saturday morning for one month instead. If it's still three, we stop and put you on homework help."
Ulla sighed, then smiled. "Fair. You've got the numbers."

qa.q: What three records did Priscila spread across the table?
qa.a: Attendance from the sign-in book, the Friday maths quiz scores and the children's feedback cards.

qa.q: What might Ulla have been feeling when she asked if they were keeping chess?
qa.a: She was probably nervous and a little protective, because the chess hour was hers and the numbers could mean it would end.

qa.q: Why is a one-month trial a better choice than stopping chess at once?
qa.a: It gives the activity a fair chance to recover under a new time, and the same monthly numbers will show clearly whether to keep or stop it.

qa.q: How might the children who come to homework help be affected by these monthly checks?
qa.a: They benefit, because effort goes where attendance and quiz scores show it is working, and more volunteers may join their group.

grounding: It shows an organiser checking attendance, quiz scores and feedback each month to decide whether to continue, adjust or stop an activity.

subtopic: Planning a legacy or purpose project
passage:
The noticeboard in the Tolichowki community centre had a new chart every month. Vinita, who ran the Saturday coding class, filled it in herself. Rows for each activity: coding, spoken English, the art corner. Columns for how many came, the end-of-month test average, and the tally of thumbs-up and thumbs-down slips.
In the September review, Zainab, a second-year volunteer, read the English row aloud. "Attendance fell from twenty-two to nine. Slips say it clashes with Friday prayers."
"Then the problem is the timing, not the class," Vinita said. "Test scores for the nine who came are good."
She moved English to Sunday afternoon. The art corner, which had full attendance but no tests, stayed as it was.
In October the chart showed English back at twenty. Zainab drew a small star beside it on the board.

qa.q: How far did attendance in the English class fall?
qa.a: Attendance fell from twenty-two to nine.

qa.q: How can you tell Zainab felt pleased in October?
qa.a: She drew a small star beside the English row after the chart showed attendance back at twenty, showing she was proud and relieved. 😊

qa.q: What would you change first if the English attendance had not come back after the move?
qa.a: I would talk to a few of the students who stopped coming, because the slips give a clue but a short conversation could show a reason the numbers miss.

qa.q: How do the students who pray on Fridays experience Vinita's change?
qa.a: They no longer have to choose between prayers and class, so they may feel included and more willing to keep coming.

grounding: It shows an organiser using monthly attendance, test averages and feedback slips to decide which activity to keep, move or leave as it is.
